MR. CHOQUETTE-REPORTED SPEECH BY MEMBER FOR PORT ARTHUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, as a result of a speech delivered in Toronto by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), in which he said that the province of Quebec was the greatest obstacle to a comprehensive vision and a common effort in federal politics. He said:
The Quebec members of parliament tend to stand aloof from their colleagues speaking the other language and to consider their provincial capital as the real seat of power in Canada.
Such statements, Mr. Speaker, are unfair and unfortunate and cannot but deeply annoy the Quebec members in this house.
The main political concern of every Canadian citizen should be the greatness and prestige of Canada.
Quebec members are Canadians and are prompted by that national political ideal. Of course, they refuse to be assimilated because they are prompted by a true national ideal, which is based on their will to spread the influence of the French fact throughout Canada.
We categorically reject the statements made by the hon. member for Port Arthur and we declare that, contrary to the ideology preached by the Liberal federation of Quebec and its officers, the main political expression of French Canada is the Quebec members sitting in the House of Commons who wish to contribute to the greatness of their country, of which they are proud.

Mr. Speaker, today the Canadian wheat board announced in Winnipeg that it has negotiated a contract for the sale
of approximately 100,000 long tons of wheat to Hungary. This sale, totalling about 3.7 million bushels, is for shipment during the period December through March, 1965, from Canadian east coast ports. This is the first sale made to Hungary under the provisions of the long term agreement signed on June 11, 1964, whereby Hungary had agreed to purchase 250,000 long tons of wheat during the three years of the agreement.
Payment for the wheat is to be made on the basis of ten per cent at time of shipment with the remaining balance to be paid in equal instalments, plus interest, at two, two and a half and three years respectively. These credit arrangements were authorized by the government of Canada under the provisions of the Export Credits Insurance Act. The buyer has the right to divert the wheat to any other eastern European socialist country.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-134, respecting the national game of Canada (lacrosse).

speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: DESIGNATION OF LACROSSE AS CANADA'S NATIONAL GAME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I read the preamble to the bill and the explanatory notes, both of which are very brief, I think this will explain the purpose of the bill. The preamble reads:

Questions
Whereas lacrosse has been played in Canada from time immemorial; whereas it has long been assumed that lacrosse is the national game of Canada; and whereas there is an attempt to have a lesser game adopted as the national game of Canada-
The explanatory notes read:
Lacrosse has been played in Canada for an unknown period of time, having been played by the original native Indian people. It is uniquely Canadian and was not imported to this country [DOT]as all other games have been.
The purpose of this bill is to rectify what was probably an oversight on the part of the Fathers of Confederation who were so preoccupied with drafting sections 91 and 92 of the B.N.A. Act that the question of declaring a national game escaped their attention.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for New Westminster has seconded this bill not simply because he is my seatmate, but he represents the home city of the Salmonbellies, which team has won the Canadian senior lacrosse championship more times than any other team.

1. The terms of reference for the committee on occurrence of congenital abnormalities, as set out in the minutes of the meeting of the dominion council of health in April 1963, are as follows:-
"The purpose of the committee shall be to advise the Department of National Health and Welfare, through the dominion council of health, on measures which when implemented will improve the quantity, quality and availability of information on the occurrence of congenital anomalies in Canada.
This information shall be pertinent to etiology, prevention, diagnosis and ultimately the treatment and rehabilitation of individuals so affected.
This information shall be of such a nature as to be of value for epidemiological studies, assessment of health service needs, as well as more fundamental research in the field of etiology.
The committee shall examine currently available information from various sources and shall determine its adequacy for the above purposes.
The committee may establish subcommittees to study particular aspects of the problem and may add to its membership, if necessary, for this purpose."

Will the minister indicate what procedure the government has in mind, and his department in particular, to assure that each Indian band, reserve and tribe in this country will have a right to vote on whether they want a change in their relationship with the federal

Inquiries of the Ministry government or its control over them, and when will the vote take place? In general, what is going to be done or what is envisaged to assure that the Indians will not be pushed around as chattels?

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subsubtopic: METHOD OF CONSULTATION RESPECTING CHANGES IN RELATIONSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that the hon. Leader of the Opposition asked me this question which will allow me, after the federal-provincial conference which was held here Thursday and Friday last and which was quite successful, to give clarifying explanations concerning the consulting procedure which was agreed upon at that conference.
The first point upon which the participants to that conference agreed upon was the necessity of consulting the Indians concerning any program which might affect them in the future.
This consulting procedure will operate at two levels.
First, in every province of Canada there shall be held a conference to which all Indians will be invited so they can express their wishes and their suggestions on the very principle of extending provincial services to the Indians in every province. After this consultation and provided the Indians agree that such provincial services would be desirable, there shall be a second method consultation: the bands will be consulted. Every band in Canada or in every province will be consulted-that is, the councils of those bands will be consulted in order to ascertain if they wish to take advantage of a program to be established in a province, and every band which does not wish to take advantage of provincial services will be free to reject such services and, under those circumstances, the federal services will remain in force.
This double consultation will make the federal and provincial governments aware of the feelings and wishes of the Indian population concerning the provision of services by the provinces.
Third, it was decided at the conference to set up, in each province, a standing Indian affairs committee which will be consulted on any administrative question concerning the Indians. As can be seen, at the very first official meeting the federal government and the provinces have been able to agree on machinery which will ensure adequate consultations with the Indians in the future.
For the first time the Indians will feel that they will be the first to benefit from the steps
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)
taken by the government and that far from seeking to impose its decisions upon them, the latter wishes to approve steps which they themselves would consider advantageous.

Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock on Friday I was briefly pointing out to the committee the undesirable situation in which the Yukon and Northwest Territories find themselves at present by not having full representation in parliament. I had made the point that although for the first time since 1962 the Canadian northland had members of parliament, the situation had not yet been corrected in terms of representation in the other place. I had made the point that at the present time there are in excess of 40,000 Canadian citizens living north of the 60th parallel, yet neither the Yukon nor the Northwest Territories had been allowed representation in the other place. I believe I made the point that even though there may be historical reasons, a province such as Prince Edward Island with a population of 107,000 had four senatorial representatives in parliament. It seems to me that the political development of our northern areas warrants this move.
One need only think back to last year, when we had legislation in this chamber intended to divide the Northwest Territories into two separate parts. Presumably that was going to be a step in the political evolution of that area. As another example of just how unsure of itself this government is, I point out that that proposed legislation was sent to a committee, and we have heard nothing about it since. Nor has the government reintroduced that measure.
Mr. Chairman, I mention these facts because I intend to give notice that at the time the formula for repatriating the constitution is brought before the house I will expect the government to have some sort of plan ready along the lines I have mentioned. It seems to me this would be the logical course of development, not only in terms of the political evolution of the Northwest Territories but also to ensure that all Canada is fully represented in parliament. This can

only be done if the Yukon and Northwest Territories are allowed representation in the other place.
I do not know what answer the government can give at the present time for overlooking this matter during the last 18 months, nor am I particularly interested in that answer. I hope all hon. members of this house will support me when I say that in a few months' time it will be completely unacceptable to us as Canadians to have the government bring in a formula for amending the constitution without first having taken the steps necessary to give the Yukon and Northwest Territories full representation in parliament.
Mr. Chairman, I am not a constitutional lawyer, but I did listen very carefully to the debate on Friday, and it seems to me that at the present time the federal government has the authority to create a province or provinces in the Canadian northland. If the proposed formula is adopted then it will require two thirds of the provinces, including either Quebec or Ontario, before the federal authority can create a new province. Speaking as the member for the Northwest Territories I can assure this committee that for several reasons the implications of such a formula are frightening. They are frightening because the present federal government has never shown any interest in the north country. Certainly that has caused a great deal of distrust and will remain the source of distrust as long as the present Minister of Finance holds that portfolio. One need only think back a few years, when that individual headed a royal commission on Canadian economic prospects, and stated in effect that if people living in the maritimes could not make a go of it they should move to Toronto. In other words his solution to the problems facing people who live in depressed areas is for those people to move out. He certainly wrote off that 60 per cent of Canada which lies north of the 55th parallel, as having any real future as far as our economy is concerned.
If the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory are to be dependent upon the whim of one province, let us say Quebec, for example, before they are allowed full economic and political status, they will find themselves in an impossible position. If one thinks back a few months he will realize that the present government made great political capital everywhere in the southern part of this country by accusing the previous administration of throwing away thousands of dollars in the northland. There is no doubt in my mind that the
Interim Supply
Liberal government won hundreds of thousands of votes in the southern area of Canada by writing off the Yukon and Northwest Territories. That is a frightening situation. My colleague the hon. member for Yukon is unavoidably absent today, but I can assure this committee that he also is alarmed by this situation.
In the last two days we have seen examples of what can happen to us if we become dependent upon the good graces of the other provinces in Canada. For example, one can easily imagine the difficulties we might encounter if we had to obtain the approval of the province of Quebec before provinces could be created out of either the Yukon or Northwest Territories; and that would be the situation should the suggested formula be adopted. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the province of Quebec has expressed a great deal of interest in the offshore islands which lie immediately adjacent to the coast of that province. One can easily envisage the sort of blackmail position in which we could find ourselves in the Northwest Territories if we were seeking full political status as a province, having to obtain concurrence of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I am not discussing the merits of the suggestion that the offshore islands should belong to Quebec.

speechtext: Order, please. Perhaps I will be allowed to bring to the attention of hon. members that there are many conversations being carried on in this chamber, and that it is very difficult to follow the hon. member who has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. For the benefit of those who did not hbar what I said because of a preoccupation with a little caucus across the way, I suggested that the offshore islands off the coast of Quebec, which at the present time are considered a part of the Northwest Territories, might well for administrative purposes, or for all purposes, belong to the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

Indeed, I personally support such a suggestion, because I think it would make geographic sense. As hon. members may realize, the problem exists because when the boundaries of the Northwest Territories were being determined they were not determined in terms of co-ordinates or metes and bounds, but in terms of high water marks. When one considers the straits which

Interim Supply
separate Baffin land from Quebec and realizes that at times and in places the tide there is in excess of 60 feet, he can see what happens when the tide goes out. All the land that is exposed belongs to the Northwest Territories. This is an illogical situation and should be corrected. I know my hon. friend from Lapointe has pressed for this before, but I am merely using this as an example of the sort of problem that would occur should it be necessary for the federal government to obtain the consent of two thirds of the provinces, including either Quebec or Ontario, in order to create a new province in the northland.
There is one other current problem worthy of mention in this context. Only a few weeks ago the premier of British Columbia expressed a new found interest in annexing the Yukon territory and part of Mackenzie territory. That was not a laughing matter, or considered as a joke. Nor was it a display of the bad manners of the newly rich by Mr. Bennett.
It was not just an attempt on his part to become prime minister by buying up Canada even though we know he already has $100 million worth of Quebec in his pocket. It was a serious move on his part to take over a large section of Canada. He too recognizes the policy and planning vacuum that has existed in the Northwest Territories since the change of government. He knows that nothing new has been initiated by the Liberal government in the last two years. He knows that the people of the Yukon and Mackenzie districts are discontented because of the neglect they have experienced once again at the hands of a Liberal government.
If the premier of British Columbia had said two years ago that he wanted to take over the Yukon and part of the Northwest Territories he would have been laughed at throughout the country, and to the people who live in the territories it would have been unthinkable. However, today in both the Yukon and the Mackenzie districts there are people who are seriously pondering the offer made by Premier Bennett. They are doing so because they have come to the conclusion that the present federal government has no interest in developing the area and has not retained the impetus initiated by the previous administration, and therefore they had better give serious consideration to the offer made by the premier of British Columbia.
The people who live in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories do not intend to be pawns in federal-provincial conferences in

the future. Why should our status from the point of view of being provinces be dependent upon the acquisitiveness of various provincial premiers who recognize that in Ottawa at the present time there is a weak federal leader and that this is an appropriate time for them to swoop in because they know that all their demands will be met? We in the territories are most alarmed over the policy followed by the present government of yielding to whatever pressures are exerted. We are alarmed because we are totally dependant on the federal authority for the time being, and if at the bargaining table the only thing the federal government is going to consider is political strength you can imagine how we in the north' feel with only one lonesome member from the Yukon and another from the Northwest Territories. Only two federal seats are at stake, and if the government intends to follow a policy of responding only to political pressure related to the distribution of seats you can imagine our alarm and concern with regard to the situation.

The subject we are discussing this afternoon and which was discussed on Friday is one that was raised by members on this side at the first opportunity because of certain events that occurred in mid October. I make no apology at all for participating in the debate on the question of the amendment of the constitution. I make no pretence whatsoever of being a constitutional expert, but in the light of the comments that are being made with greater and greater frequency throughout the country I must say it is incumbent upon us to raise questions about these highly important events which took place in mid October.
We all know that Her Majesty was here prior to the 15th of October, and that on that particular day a communique was issued by the federal government and the provincial premiers dealing with the matter of the amendment and patriation of the constitution. Stripped of its aura of self satisfaction the communique was more than ever unenlightening. Therefore we must ask questions in regard to this matter.
There was an attempt the other day by the Minister of Transport to say that we were wrong in raising these questions. He said that the hon. member for Bow River, the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Queens were wrong in posing questions about this matter because the formula, he claimed, was the self-same formula as in 1961, with no changes. This I question. I have very great reservations with regard to the equality of positions as between 1961 and now. Even if there is a similarity with 1961 in certain respects, and there is, it must be remembered that the proposals were made within a conference and that while certain details of the negotiations did get out, no document was deposited in the house to indicate any agreement. Actually we are being presented with a fait accompli.
In that regard I would refer to a story under the byline of Anthony Westell which appeared in the Globe and Mail of October 22. I disagree entirely with Mr. Westell's conclusion in his last paragraph. He is expressing his opinion and I disagree with it, but I will say he is factually correct when he says that within the last two years there has arisen what might be called a form of superparliament, if one can really use the word "parliament" with regard to dominion-provincial conferences. A fourth level of government has crept into the picture, because there have been any number of dominion-provincial conferences at which major agree-
Interim Supply
ments were made which were then presented to the house as something already binding upon the house because the government was bound.
We have yet to discuss the implications, in regard to the pension plan, of the step taken last April. It was a very quiet, under the table, cloak and dagger sort of proposition. Ministers at Quebec were going in the back door while other ministers were going out the front door, neither knowing that the others were present. Provinces were not being consulted beforehand and were being presented with agreements to such an extent that Premier Robarts has now said we must bring a halt to this type of procedure.
In so far as this parliament is concerned, we are now being presented with an agreement, and gracious only knows what would be the implications if this parliament were not to accept this agreement between the federal government and the provinces or were to amend it in some major particular. I must say that I believe it is all right to consult on matters of this kind, but the hands of this parliament must not be bound. I think it is high time hon. members raised this question. Quoting one paragraph from the article by Mr. Westell:
Federal-provincial conferences are becoming the real seats of power-the places at which national

In his remarks on Friday afternoon the hon. member for Bow River-I have not got the page of Hansard immediately before me -made some reference to Canada being the first nation in the whole British commonwealth to enjoy full religious liberty. I would point out to hon. gentlemen, and this is a very brief run through of history, that if we look back to pre-1763, the inhabitants of Canada, whether they were Roman Catholic or Huguenot, enjoyed the same rights of freedom of worship and security of properties. With the treaty of Paris in 1763 these same rights were guaranteed to Roman Catholics. They were confirmed by the Quebec Act in 1791, and they were extended to the new province of Upper Canada with the act of union just a few years later.
In the year following, with the passage of the Roman Catholic emancipation bill, all disabilities for Roman Catholics were removed in the remaining portions of Canada, that is the maritime provinces. This is a recognized fact that is all too frequently forgotten. Under the aegis of Westminster we have enjoyed in this country full religious liberty without the disabilities that applied for so many years even in Britain. I hope, therefore, that hon. members will correct their estimation of the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River in the early part of his speech on Friday afternoon.
Let us look at the proposed amendment to the constitution. Briefly, if we look at the categories under the formula we find there is, first of all, the 100 per cent consent of the provinces for the federal parliament to amend provisions of the constitution relating to (a) the powers of the legislature of a province to make laws; (b) the rights or privileges guaranteed or secured by the constitution of Canada to the legislature or government of a province; (c) the assets or properties of a province; (d) the use of the English or French language and, further, the senatorial floor or representation of a province in the House of Commons. Almost in the same category is the right of a province to-deal with education, except that Newfoundland is in a class by itself. This province

cannot have anything to say about education generally, and no other provinces can have anything to say about education in the province of Newfoundland. This is a result of the confederation act of 1949.
There is another category in which the amendment would affect one or more but not all the provinces, and in this case only those affected would have to give their consent. Almost all the remaining amendments must be concurred in by legislatures of at least two thirds of the provinces representing at least 50 per cent of the population of Canada according to the latest general census. We know that there are entrenched areas and that they are of long standing. It is agreed also that if you have amendments that affect only certain provinces, then those provinces should consent. This has been accepted. What I am concerned about is this two thirds of the provinces representing 50 per cent of the population.
It was indicated the other day that this was not the essence of the formula of 1961. In 1961 there was no proposal to do away with section 91(1) which had been passed in 1949. Yet if we examine the proposal I put it to hon. members that it goes much further, because the first numbered paragraph of the proposed constitution of Canada amendment act reads as follows:
Subject to this part, the parliament of Canada may make laws repealing, amending or re-enacting any provision of the constitution of Canada.
In other words that is the paragraph granting the maximum of power. Then all the exceptions follow, and they are legion. Under paragraph 2 we have seen that the four points, the entrenched clauses, are included in section 2, and section 3 deals with the case of "less than all of the provinces," and with the case where the affected provinces must all give their consent. Section 4 deals with education, but section 5 says this:
No law made under the authority of this part,
The language is clear and unequivocal.

In case anyone has any illusions as to how much this means, he has only to turn to the British North America Act where it will be found that the executive government of Canada is covered by sections 9 to 16 of that act, and even there some seven-no, eight- limitations have been introduced to this exclusive right of jurisdiction, and they are in part those that were included previously in section 91(1),

Mr. Chairman, it is not often in the house that we are considering an action of the government which offers an appropriate stepping-stone for us all to take a look at the general trend of government action over the last while, to see whether there is any pattern emerging out of government action, to note the behaviour of the government and the provinces, what its present effect is on Canada and whether it gives any indication as to where similar action is likely to lead us in the future.
I certainly think that when the government has announced that it has reached an agreement with the provinces on a method of amending the constitution, all of us who take seriously our responsibilities as members of the Canadian House of Commons should discuss this question in a very broad terms and try the best we can to see whether there is any trend as to where we are going, with the piecemeal legislation that now and then comes up. I am sure we are all aware that now and then the government takes a step, or a measure is passed, which seems to nibble away at a freedom, which seems to limit the economic activity of certain people; and many times we shrug it off and say, "Well, it is necessary for the greatest good at this time that some slight inconvenience be experienced". But such nibbling away does add up to a general erosion of freedom; it can mean the weakening of the country as a whole, and certainly a gradual limitation of the power of the federal government to effect the economic welfare of the people of Canada generally can lead to the impotence of the government.
While this measure is not before us directly, I think now is a good time to take

a look at the various factors which I believe are important, to get us in the state of mind in which we can properly consider the importance of the change in the constitution. Certainly many members have already indicated that they feel this agreement with the provinces amounts to a further reduction in the power of the federal government. I suggest that all of us should look seriously right now at how much power the federal government has and how much power it has to have. I get the feeling sometimes that because we have had so much pressure from the provinces we have been altogether too preoccupied with the growing responsibilities of the provinces and their inability to cope with these responsibilities out of limited resources. Also they have not seriously enough considered the fact that federal responsibility is growing, while federal capacity for action and influence on all these factors has been eroded away, and not just by giving in to the provinces.
When confederation started I am sure most of us would have agreed that the Fathers of Confederation laid great emphasis on the necessity for having a strong central government. They did not give to the provinces those fields which had the greatest influence on Canada's economic status or which gave the provincial governments the power to have a great influence on Canada's economic status. At that time it was the internal problems of the provinces-the problems of vast distance, the immaturity of the nation, etc.-which made them see clearly why the federal government, if it were to bind together such a loose confederation of provinces, had to have the main power in its hands. I suggest that if we are to approach the problem today it behooves us to look and see whether those factors have been changed so much that the same thinking does not still apply.
It is true that today we are in a much different world from the world of a hundred years ago, but I suggest that each other nation in the world today is in a different position too. Let us look at some of the outside factors which show that power has been taken away from the federal government, its capacity to manage, to conduct and influence the economic welfare of the people in the country. Trade situations have changed. We are now more than ever depending on international trade, balance of payments, tariff agreements and such general agreements as GATT. Each one of those limits the capacity of the federal government to be able freely to influence the destiny of our own people. Every 20220-612i

I suggest that we consider what has happened in Europe, where nations with much longer established governments, with in many cases much larger populations, governments without our problems of vast distances, transportation and difference of climate to contend with, nations with vast pools of skilled labour to call upon, much experience in industrialized machinery, in all of which we are just acquiring experience, have themselves found it was not within the legislative competence of their own governments to influence enough their own economic chances for survival, let alone spreading it down through the subdivisions or sections of the country. The federal governments of such countries have not had the power, acting alone, to be of sufficient use to private entrepreneurs within their own countries, so as to keep up with the cry for a rising standard of living, but have found it necessary to give some of their own economic independence to an economic union. Certainly Canada as a country has as many problems as any of these nations to which I have referred. We are blessed with perhaps a certain greater natural wealth in this country. But we do not have the wealth of manpower. We do not have the skills of some of them, and we do have the disadvantage of great distance.
I suggest that any thinking person who considers that other nations of the world have become more and more preoccupied with economic union, are spending more and more time trying to negotiate satisfactory trade agreements, have tried to bolster the purchasing power underdeveloped countries and tried to work out a lessening of tariff barriers, etc., so that the federal governments in those countries may give some assistance to their industrialists, will come to the conclusion that we would be very shortsighted indeed not to take every opportunity we have to give our federal government the chance to be of influence in that type of work.
I think that one of our major difficulties has always been the increasing demand for social justice, each of the provinces finding itself beset with new and increasing demands

The present government has been politically disappointing along this line. Certainly if we are going to consider taking away any further power from the federal government we must also consider the problems the federal government will have to meet, and whether those powers are sufficient to meet those problems. I for one believe that most people in this country are Canadians first. We must be wary of giving economic powers to the provinces, because we should

We are aware that communist nations use the governments themselves as trading agencies. If we are going to give some of the economic authority in Canada to the provincial governments in order that the provinces may take a purely regional and local approach to the economic situation we are going to be very shortsighted.
The economic problems in Canada are such that all the assistance and help the federal government has been able to give private enterprise in the past has proved in many cases to be inadequate. Should we complicate the matter by giving extra legislative competence to provincial governments which will move in the direction of assisting only those industries within the province? I am sure such a situation would result in industries within the borders of one province having a great advantage over competing industries in another province. In contrasting the conditions of government within one province with those within another we can at this time find situations where concessions given by provincial governments are almost tantamount to tariff barriers. Mr. Chairman, while we are dealing with the interim supply, I wish, like some other colleagues, to express certain views regarding a problem of capital importance, that of Canadian unity.
I take this occasion to comment on some statements made by certain of my colleagues. I hasten to add that these are colleagues whom, I admit, are competent and of good faith and whose opinions I respect also. I hope that they also will respect my views and that they will let me express them as clearly as possible.
Three very interesting questions have been raised in regard to the constitution during this debate.
It has been said, if I am not mistaken, that confederation act was not an agreement and, in short, that it was an ordinary piece of legislation just like any other. It was added, however, that when the British North America Act was passed by the British parliament, as it was wont to do, it was necessary to remove any suggestion of an agreement.
I am against the concept that the British North America Act would only be a mere piece of legislation. I maintain that it was an agreement binding the provinces in a union based on the good faith of the two main ethnic groups then constituting the Canadian people.
The B.N.A. Act is, in the tradition of British public law, on the same footing as the great pieces of British legislation which are the very basis of the personal freedoms and even of our western civilization.
I have in mind for instance, the Magna Carta, the 1689 Bill of Rights, the petition of rights and all the others. In order to convince oneself that in the minds of all the participants who united the North American colonies in 1867 an agreement was really being entered into, only one has to read the discussions held in the British House of Commons at that time. One can read, for instance, the words of the sponsor of this legis-
[Mr. Caouette.l
lation in the British parliament, Lord Carnarvon, who stated:
To those resolutions-
He was referring to the Quebec and Charlottetown resolutions, which have resulted in the adoption of the act itself.
To those resolutions, the British provinces of North America gave their consent, and the measures based upon those resolutions must be accepted as a union treaty.
Then it was said that this was an essential pact. And, if we look at it closely, we realize that such was the case, because if it had been merely a piece of legislation of the British parliament, why would the consent of the participating provinces have been required previously? Why would not all the British provinces have been united, even those which had not given their consent?
It is therefore obvious that the constituting act of our constitutional existence is a pact and was considered as such by the Canadian participants themselves, the Fathers of Con-feration, and by the British legislators. In addition, the main judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada and, especially, of the judicial committee of the privy council all confirm the theory of a pact between the provinces but mostly between the two ethnical groups. In fact, for nearly a century no French Canadian living in Quebec or elsewhere has ever thought that it was anything but a freely accepted union of all to form a new entity, Canada. Under the circumstances, there could have been no question of either direct or indirect coercion or domination.
Mr. Chairman, some astounding things have been said. It has been claimed that some plot had been contrived and reference was even made to an assassination, for words of exceptional violence have been uttered in the course of this debate on the constitution, one which surely should be marked by levelheadedness and complete objectivity. It was said that the present government had contrived a sinister plot to abdicate its responsibilities in order to decentralize constitutional and administrative authority in this country and, as a result, achieve the dissolution and disintegration of confederation itself.
I have made my share of speeches in this house and never to speak on behalf or uphold the cause of the present federal government. If any charge could be laid against this government, I would rather accuse it of being a centralizing government striving under the guise of that co-operative federalism formula, to deprive the provinces of much of their powers. Therefore, I say that there

does not seem to exist any immediate or remote conspiracy to take away from the central government any of its legitimate powers. On the other hand, decentralization in itself is not by any means a bad thing, on the contrary.
By the way, may I say very frankly and very openly at this stage of my remarks that I am in favour of a united Canada, that I have confidence and hope in the future of confederation. And, in my capacity as the authorized spokesman for the Quebec caucus of our party, I add that like the provincial leader of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), we on this side of the house do not consider that we have been given a mandate to take away from the present federal power its legitimate rights.
If we acted any differently, we would not then truly understand where our duty lies. Still, I must say we are aware that, if confederation is to continue and progress, if it is to rally the support of the majority in Canada and more especially in the province of Quebec we must face present realities, and especially that which implies recognition of the French fact, of the legitimate aspirations of the French group as an essential partner in confederation. As such, we must endorse and support as much as possible, and with all the constitutional means of which we can avail ourselves, the autonomist attitude adopted by almost all the governments of the province of Quebec, whether Liberal, Conservative, Union Nationale or other.
Mr. Chairman, were it not for such an autonomist attitude, confederation could not survive. This is not a Quebec problem only; it is a national problem, because Canada is not only composed of two main ethnic groups coming from two founding races, it comprises also many other ethnic groups. There is, in this vast geographical territory called Canada, many different economic and geographical areas which, in order to survive, must have powers which, within their jurisdiction, are completely autonomist, independent and free from any interference by the central power.
Mr. Chairman, there is another argument to support the claims of the partisans of provincial autonomy:	the transformation
within confederation and throughout the country in the last few years, especially since the last world war.
Everyone knows that under cover of the war and of the economic needs resulting therefrom, the central government monopolized as never before nearly all the powers
Interim Supply
and the economic sinews in the country. On the other hand, since the war the wind of decentralization started blowing and the provinces, having under the constitution sovereign powers in their own field, acquired responsibilities which they never had before and were faced with all sorts of needs. Now, to carry out their responsibilities in these fields, the provinces had to have fiscal means which, largely under cover of the war and also for other but less obvious reasons, were monopolized by the central power; the provinces have been claiming these fiscal resources since the end of the war. I am thinking, for instance, about their responsibility in the fields of public education, communications within the provinces, municipal services, social welfare and particularly about the development of national resources of all provinces. Those are concrete tasks, tremendous responsibilities the provinces must assume and that is why there was a whole series of federal-provincial conferences during which all premiers spoke with one voice in order to give back to the appropriate jurisdiction the means to legitimately carry out the obligations incumbent to them under the constitution. And I think that such a trend will certainly continue.
There was much more. Since the end of the war-it is proper to say so-there has been a new awakening in the province of Quebec, and especially among French Canadians. Quebec is now conscious of its power and of its human as well as material resources. I think it is accurate to say that the great majority of its population, having such resources, want to use them for legitimate purposes and to promote its development in all fields, so that it can be strong, more powerful and more united to share in this great Canadian achievement.
I think that such is the true voice and desire of the moderate elements in the province of Quebec. I leave out of consideration all those who, because of past disappointments, have lost their illusions, and no longer believe in the possibility of the existence of a confederation where their rights would be fully recognized.
Mr. Chairman, I think that while desiring national unity, we must demand from our government leaders, from all those who have responsibilities, to pursue a genuine Canadian policy and I cannot see the pursuit of such a policy without the implementation of a great many reforms, the need of which is getting more pressing day by day.
I am thinking in particular of the necessity for our country to approve a truly distinctive

Interim Supply
flag. I am for this distinctive flag, Mr. Chairman. I, for one, am quite satisfied that a committee looked into this matter for nearly two months and held a great many meetings at the end of which it finally made its choice. I recognize that this choice has been freely accepted by the majority of the members on this committee, and I feel that to delay the approval of the committee's report, at this stage, would certainly not help the cause of national unity.
I also believe that legislation concerning the repatriation of the constitution should be passed quickly. I have examined the two formulae:	the one brought forth in 1961
and the 1964 version. I am unable to see any essential difference between the two, or at least, no difference in respect of the federal government powers. Even if this formula is examined carefully with a magnifying glass, nowhere will there be found a lessening of federal powers. Therefore, it seems that when one is speaking of a plot, in this repatriation formula, in order to get rid of certain powers of the federal government, this assertion cannot be proved by the text that was submitted.
Certainly, there are differences. Sections 6, 7, 8, and part 3 of the press release or legislative project are different from the Fulton formula of 1961. But nowhere is there any lessening of the powers of the central government, except in section 6 which contains a definition of what constitutes federal jurisdiction, and also certain powers under which the federal government could not unilaterally make any amendment.
This is why, Mr. Chairman, I feel that it is advisable to adopt quickly and without acrimony the necessary address in order to bring home the constitution in accord with the wishes of most Canadians and of the British authorities themselves.
I also believe that once we have brought home the constitution, we should also think of revising and modernizing it. It is not difficult to realize that the British North America Act and some other statutes that are part of our constitution are antiquated, rigid, and do not meet the realities of today.
It is only normal that after 100 years there should be this anxiety to modernize an instrument which certainly served us well in the past but is no longer adequate in the light of today's needs. And when I say today's needs, I do not mean only the legitimate claims and aspirations of only a section of the population, namely the French Canadian people, but I mean also all social, economic and cultural problems which are not men-

tioned in the constitution and for which a solution does not seem to be provided.
In my opinion, those are facts about which we, the members of the Canadian parliament, must think seriously.
We live in a changing world, and Mr. Chairman, the very basis of the British genius is to accept changes when they become necessary. Where would the British commonwealth of nations be today if the British genius had not changed with the times, accepted changes, and created a large association of free nations which are an important factor in the peace and prosperity of the world?
Mr. Chairman, the world we live in is an independent world, and it is certain that no matter under which system we live we will still be subject to that interdependence between all the nations of the world and will have to accept it.
In my opinion, to refuse changes when their necessity has become absolutely obvious and clear is to show a lack of flexibility, a lack of political realism.
One of the greatest virtues which made the western civilization great is tolerance, and I believe that we, the members of parliament, while considering today and in the following days our very future, will have to show much tolerance. If we consider the problems I mentioned in that spirit we will find a solution and Canada will become a greater nation.

Mr. Chairman, I was not able to be in the house last week but I have been checking the Hansard record to see what subjects were under discussion at that time. I was interested to discover that most of the complaints which were presented in the committee with respect to government action, or lack of action, related to a problem that I was exposed to directly last week during my absence from the house. It was my privilege to attend the opening of parliament in another commonwealth country, the island of Bermuda. I was interested to note the different functions of parliament as they exist here compared with those in a parliamentary body which has not yet completed the transition from representative parliamentary democracy to responsible parliamentary democracy.
It was also interesting to note that the Bermuda parliament had some of the problems with which we are faced in this country. As a matter of fact the newly formed oppo-

sition in that country decided to demonstrate its protest against the policies of the administration by boycotting the opening ceremonies of parliament. As I have been listening to the groans and moans emanating from the government benches this afternoon as opposition members have risen to their feet to take part in this important discussion on interim supply I have come to the conclusion that some of my hon. friends across the way might hope that the opposition in the Canadian House of Commons would demonstrate its protest by being absent from the sittings of the committee.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Most of them are right now.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that most of them are absent at the moment from the sittings of parliament. I am always surprised when a member of his broad experience in parliament makes a comment of that kind, because he has been in the house long enough to know that members of parliament have other responsibilities than those which bring them to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Oh, that line.

I know my hon. friend is always aware that this will get him a headline and I suppose that is why he makes these frequent interjections into our parliamentary discussions here.
Before I was interrupted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I was pointing out, Mr. Chairman, that judging from the reaction of members opposite they might wish that the members of the opposition would discharge their responsibilities by being absent from this chamber. It seems to me that that would demonstrate the attitude I saw in the Bermuda parliament, which has not yet completed the transition from representative democracy to responsible democracy.
In this regard I should like to make some comments on the discussion which took place last week on the subject of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Again?

Mr. Chairman, hon. members keep interjecting from across the way. Unfortunately I cannot hear their mumblings so therefore am unable to reply. However, I make this comment just in case the Hansard reporter has been able to catch their mumblings, instead of their rising to their feet and discussing intelligently these important subjects.
Interim Supply
I think that by failing to recognize that we do have responsible democracy in Canada the government brings trouble upon its own head. As I read the discussion which took place about the C.B.C., member after member made the point that it would be in the best interests of our parliamentary process if the subject of the C.B.C. were brought before a parliamentary committee. This house of course is the highest court of public opinion in the land. Whenever the government is questioned on the functions of the
C.B.C. it always replies that that important public corporation is responsible to the parliament of Canada. If that is so, Mr. Chairman, how can parliament discharge its responsibility better than by having an opportunity to hear from representatives of the C.B.C. before a parliamentary committee? In addition, we as members would have an opportunity to make comments and suggestions to the officials of the corporation in the process of discussion in a parliamentary committee.
This was the practice when I first came into parliament back in the early 1950's. There was a parliamentary committee on broadcasting almost every second year and it led to some of the useful reforms brought about in this house in 1958. But this government, in its stubborn refusal to refer such a difficult and complex subject to a parliamentary committee on broadcasting, brings trouble down upon its own head. This seems to be typical of the actions of the present government in handling the affairs of the nation, and certainly in handling the affairs of parliament: its failure to present business in an orderly fashion, and its introducing divisive subjects in an arbitrary manner.
In this connection I make merely a passing reference to the flag, which has so disrupted and confused the deliberations of this body during the current session of parliament. They knew by introducing a divisive subject of this kind that this would be the inevitable result. In its failure to allow representatives from the C.B.C. to come before a parliamentary committee the government is creating difficulty as well for that body.
There is bound to be criticism of a crown corporation charged with the responsibility of carrying on a comprehensive national broadcasting service. Questions are being asked on orders of the day, cluttering up the preliminary procedures of this house. It is inevitable that on a motion for interim supply, which provides an opportunity for discussing these matters, we have an extended

Interim Supply
debate on the subject. The parliamentary committee system has been extolled as a time saving device by parliamentary reformers from all sides of this house. Yet the government has resorted to a cover-up procedure by appointing an advisory committee which will in due course report to parliament, and in this arbitrary way has by-passed the basic principle of parliament and the responsibilities of the elected representatives.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will the hon. member permit a question at this point?
Certainly.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When the hon. member mentions the C.B.C. and the reference to the advisory committee, does he not think it would be fair to comment on what was said about a parliamentary committee at the time of the announcement? He will recall that at that point there was reference made to a parliamentary committee, and that reference can be found in Hansard.

The point I am making is that instead of setting up a parliamentary committee the government has decided to set up an advisory committee which will in due course report to parliament. If we are going to adhere to the principles of responsible democracy, it is essential that the elected representatives of the people have an opportunity of reviewing from time to time the functions of this Important body.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member understood my point. In the announcement regarding the advisory committee there was a commitment made, as I recall it, that a parliamentary committee would be set up to study the recommendations of that advisory committee.

This is precisely what I am saying. The government is introducing an intermediary body. In other words the government is setting up another court of public opinion in this country to give consideration to the problems of broadcasting, and is stating that that secondary court of public opinion must report before the primary court of public opinion can take action. No democratic country can afford more than one high court of public opinion. This is our complaint and protest.
If the government had even a simple knowledge and understanding of the functions of the C.B.C. it should have been able to avoid this error. If the government had an understanding of responsible parliamentary democracy it would be aware that in order to

satisfy the interests of the members of parliament in the functions of this tremendously powerful public opinion and educational service, it would have to make it possible for direct contact between the members of parliament and the officials of this organization. That has been the practice in the past but, as I have already intimated, but for some inexplicable reason, the present government has not resorted to the established practice.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has made reference to an action taken by the government as announced on May 25, 1964, and which appears at page 3520 of Hansard. However, in referring to that announcement he has omitted to refer to a statement therein about a parliamentary committee and a time limit within which it would be set up. I am asking him whether he thinks that is a fair way of presenting his case.
Mr. Chairman, the point I am making is that an advisory committee is to be set up.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A parliamentary committee is to be set up also.

A parliamentary committee is to be set up following the recommendations of the advisory committee. The reason I have difficulty in understanding the government's devious device in this regard is because the government itself reiterates that the C.B.C. is not responsible to the government, but is responsible to parliament. What better way could it demonstrate that responsibility than by giving members of parliament an opportunity from time to time of making its wishes, comments and criticisms known with respect to the operations of this huge public corporation?
Mr. Chairman, the minister suggests that I am ignoring a statement which appears in Hansard. I am not ignoring that statement, but I am criticizing the government because a parliamentary committee is going to be bypassed in the first instance by an advisory committee which has no responsibility, or a lower level of responsibility, to the elected representatives in the House of Commons.
Various commentators have pointed out that it is unfair for members of parliament constantly to raise questions on orders of the day concerning the operations of the C.B.C. This is the only possible opportunity hon. members have to ask these questions, if the procedure which used to be followed, having the affairs of the C.B.C. submitted for review by a parliamentary committee on a regular basis, is not to be followed. Cer-

tainly discussions about an item of expenditure of some $100 million is in order during the debate on interim supply because, by the very actions of the government, we have a prime example of taxation without representation.
The government for some reason has tried to make a sacrosanct organization of the C.B.C. by removing it from the arena of public discussion. As I have already indicated, this is not only embarrassing to the government but is a source of embarrassment to the C.B.C. I think we should consider again the fundamental points which the C.B.C. reiterates in the midst of the current and continuing controversy. The C.B.C. admits that the air waves do not belong to any corporation, either private or public, but that they are a trust to be administered in the interests of the people. The air waves belong to the people. The officials of the C.B.C. also indicate that they are charged with the responsibility of carrying out broad national objectives. In this parliament we have the representatives of the people. This is the court of opinion where these broad national objectives are debated, and where we are trying to achieve a national consensus.
If we consider the early organizational period of the C.B.C. we will find that it was patterned after the British Broadcasting Corporation. The policies and techniques that had already been developed in the B.B.C. were adhered to very closely in the initial setting up of the C.B.C., and it has been pointed out over and over again in the house that the British parliament discharges its responsibility through regular referral of B.B.C. matters to a parliamentary committee at Westminster.
What are some of the main broad national objectives which make it important for parliament to have an opportunity to make its wishes known to the officials of the C.B.C.? First of all, Canadianization is the major function and role of the C.B.C. as defined in the Broadcasting Act, to encourage the development of Canadian talent, and to counter the influence of the powerful broadcasting media south of the border. We should have an opportunity to see how the C.B.C. is discharging this most important of all functions. Second, there is the question of national unity and the efforts of the C.B.C. to assist in the achieving of national unity. If we are to learn any lesson from the discussions that have been going on in the house and throughout the country in recent months, I think we will readily come to the coninterim Supply
elusion there is something wrong with the national consensus and national unity in the Canadian body politic at the present time. Therefore it would be most advisable for members of parliament to have an opportunity to see just how the C.B.C. is assisting the cause of national unity at this time through its radio and television facilities.
I have heard comments outside the house by responsible ministers of the Quebec government, for example, to the effect that the programming of the C.B.C. in recent months has tended to have a detrimental effect, rather than encouraging national unity. I refer in particular to the statement of Hon. Bona Arsenault just the other day when speaking on this subject. Mr. Arsenault is no stranger to the House of Commons. He sat in the house for many years. In his remarks the other day he was not speaking from a provincial or regional point of reference but as one who was a federal member of parliament for many years and who, if I recall correctly, took a special interest in the operations of the C.B.C. through the parliamentary committee that used to meet.
Then of course there is recurring criticism by members representing various parts of the country that there is a tendency for the national broadcasting system to have a regional bias. When we think of the development of Canadian talent we find that most of such talent is developed in the more populous areas of Canada and we sometimes hear protests raised from the less populous regions of Canada, the maritimes or the western part of the country, that the same opportunities for program origination and cultural development are not provided in the non-metropolitan areas and regions. This of course is because the large metropolitan communities tend to dominate the national life of Canada as they dominate the life of any nation.
I should like to refer to a third important function which is often cited as basic to the operations of the C.B.C. I have in mind the educational and cultural function. It is recognized that a broadcasting organization with the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation bears very important responsibility for educational and cultural development. This is reflected in the $100 million annually which is made available for its operations by the parliament of Canada.
It must also be recalled that when the C.B.C. was first organized as a federally operated institution Ottawa was very sensitive about invading the field of educational responsibility because of the jurisdictional prob-

Interim Supply
lem with which we are all too familiar and which has been a part of the discussion today on the subject of dominion-provincial relations. But back in the 1930's the government at Ottawa moved into the broadcasting field because it felt this was a most important medium for cementing Canada together and developing a sense of national unity largely through educational and cultural programming.
We in this parliament have moved quite a distance from our attitude toward educational priorities in those days. I need only refer to the grants to Canadian universities, to the amount of over $400 million that has been poured into the development of the excellent system of technical and vocational schools now available to the young people of Canada. Yet even though parliament has expanded its educational activities in other fields the fiscal demands of the C.B.C. continue to mount in an almost astronomical way. University leaders of Canada constantly remind parliament that they are being hard pressed to meet the challenge of education in the modern world because of the tremendous influx of the post-war generation of Canadians, the population explosion resulting from the war baby generation now reaching university age. It is high time that parliament gave some consideration to priorities in regard to assistance in meeting the educational problems of the nation. We grant $100 million to the C.B.C. I do not know what the figure is for federal grants to universities but obviously it has not increased in equal proportion.
As I have intimated, it was the practice to have the broadcasting committees up until the change of government in 1963. The Conservative government established a parliamentary committee to deal with broadcasting matters and the preceding Liberal government set up several parliamentary committees for this purpose. Arising out of the deliberations of the parliamentary committee in 1957 and 1958 there came very important policy recommendations which resulted in changes in broadcasting procedures that had a beneficial effect in regard to the functions of broadcasting in this nation. The B.B.G., for example, was established and it is high time an opportunity was given for an examination of that body such as is made possible through the device of a parliamentary committee. We must remember also that there has been a continuing shift from radio to television. I do not have the relative expenditures at my fingertips, but I would imagine that a large

part of the $100 million made available for the C.B.C. is designated for the telecasting function rather than the radio function.
I neglected to mention in the earlier assessment of the functions of public broadcasting in Canada that it was always emphasized that it was desirous to have adequate broadcasting services without resort to commercialization. I think we are all aware that more and more, in both the telecasting and radio fields, the C.B.C. is resorting to revenues from advertising in order to assist in financing. Here is another aspect that could be examined by a suitable parliamentary committee.
Then, we now have alternative broadcasting services available. The private stations, both radio and television, have broadened their services to the Canadian public within recent years. During the past hearings of the parliamentary committee, it has been possible for members of parliament to hear representations from the representatives of the private broadcasters. I wonder if this advisory committee the government has set up is even going to give the private broadcasters an opportunity to make their difficulties and problems known.
Then, another major item that will confront the C.B.C. and the private broadcasters, and because of parliament's function in scrutinizing the operations of the C.B.C. it will concern all members of this house, is the fact we are about to face the decision of whether or not Canada should go into the colour telecasting field. I recall that back in 1952, I believe, the parliamentary committee of that year gave attention to the question of whether or not the C.B.C. should go into the telecasting field. As a result of the discussion in the committee, the C.B.C. was able to come to a decision that was in tune with prevailing public opinion of the day. I can recall, too, we even had a discussion in that committee of whether or not it was desirable to have an FM broadcasting network that would supplement the AM broadcasting facilities at that time. Well, the recommendation came strongly from the parliamentary committee that the C.B.C. should move into FM broadcasting, and as a direct result of the deliberations of that committee the Canadian Broadcasting facilities were considerably improved.
During this debate I do not want to go into the question of programming on the C.B.C.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to interrupt the hon. member to inform him that his time has expired, unless he has unanimous consent to continue.
Agreed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman; I will not trespass for very many minutes on the patience of the committee because, as I have intimated already, I do not want to discuss, either in a positive or negative way, the programming of the C.B.C. I do not believe that this committee of the whole is the place in which this subject can be dealt with adequately. It is easy to criticize a particular program, as happens from time to time in this house. Then we hear the minister, speaking from his exalted level of non-partisanism and non-political interference, say that he would be very happy to bring the comments of the hon. members to the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. How much more useful and effective it would be if hon. members could sit across the table and make their comments about these programs and get answers directly from the C.B.C. officials. I am sure the C.B.C. officials would be pleased to explain the motivation behind some of these programs that give rise to discussion and comment not only in this house but in many parts of Canada.
It is not only a public information media such as the C.B.C. that comes under criticism. The press is always under criticism. Of course, we have more direct access to the press through the printed page, and the press is also a private information service. Unfortunately the C.B.C., as a public information body, has to consider the delicate relationships between politicians and the corporation. This makes it a very much more sensitive and difficult area in which to operate. It is not only the press that is criticized. I can recall year after year in this house discussions going forward about the problem of salacious and indecent literature, in much the same terms as the pornography on the C.B.C. comes under discussion here. It was the former member for Kamloops who kept this subject alive over a number of years in such a way that finally this parliament was persuaded to take some legislative action. I am certainly not at all in favour of censorship, but I am absolutely in favour of an expression of public opinion from this responsible parliamentary body that can make the wishes of the people of Canada known to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I have one final word on this subject, and that is to underscore the importance of a mass media of communication in the world in which we live. We know that the printed word and the earlier means of communication
Interim Supply
have had an important role to play in shaping the destinies not only of nations but of whole civilizations. I remember, for example, that well known economist, Dr. Innes, at the University of Toronto, giving a series of lectures on the subject of civilization and communication. His thesis was simply this, that the values of the civilization achieved by man in any particular period of time are strongly determined by the means of communication which are available.
He went back to the days of the Egyptian civilization, pointing out that the great leap forward was made possible by the invention of even a simple improvement in communications such as papyrus as opposed to the cuneiform writing which had been the only means of written communication up to that time. But how much more important is this thesis in the kind of world in which we live today, which has mass media able to engage in all sorts of subtle propaganda which can brainwash people without their even knowing they are being brainwashed. I refer to the hidden persuasion which is made possible by the subliminal advertising available in television, whereby one can flash a message on a screen, a message the viewer is not even aware of but which seeps into his subconscious and thus determines his behaviour and motivation.
We hear many criticisms from responsible groups that the avante garde has taken over in certain areas of the C.B.C. and are using this important mass medium to put forward their views, views which obviously are motivating many people, if we are to judge by a generation of angry young men and women making its protests heard in many national areas. All of this has been brought home to us in a forceful manner in recent weeks.
That is all I have time to say at the moment, Mr. Chairman. We have not even begun to exhaust the comments that could be made on broadcasting. I have endeavoured to put forward a case for the referral of C.B.C. and broadcasting matters to a parliamentary committee rather than resorting to the devious device of an advisory committee, such as the government has done. This is a dereliction of duty on the part of the government, because in our form of parliamentary democracy the government and the agencies operating under its aegis must always be responsible to the elected representatives of the people.

In the few minutes left before six o'clock I should like to remind the committee that when I led off the debate on

Interim Supply
interim supply on Friday, October 23, a serious problem confronted us with regard to transport. Those of us who participated in the debate were certainly gratified to note that on the following Monday certain action was taken which we hoped would make it possible for a commission to investigate the situation, but even though some work has been done, to date the situation has not been resolved.
I understand there is difficulty finding someone to head an investigative commission, and we have no guarantee on how long the railway employees will keep their contract to run and operate the trains if no positive action is taken. If, because of the inability of the government or the Minister of Transport to find someone suitable for this job, services were again disrupted, this would be most unfortunate. I sincerely hope that in the very near future a commissioner will be named to investigate the situation, and that an arrangement will be reached satisfactory to both management and the unions involved. The President of the Privy Council was good enough to say we can expect some action in this respect in the near future, but I believe such an announcement should come from the Minister of Transport who holds direct responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, before the supper hour I was trying, with limited success, to point out that the winds of constitutional change are blowing everywhere in the world, even in the British Isles, where the Scottish nationalists used some unorthodox methods of bringing their views before the public. However, having done it in a rather polite manner, they were not ostracized, as is shown by the fact that the people of Great Britain had two Scottish prime ministers prior to the recent election. While the stone of Scone, or the stone of destiny, as I mentioned, was resident in Westminster, I am one of those who feel that we are not inconvenienced to too great an extent by the residence of the constitution in Westminster; but I did feel that the repatriation of the constitution would begin a war of attrition on that constitution.
We see this because of several situations which have taken place in the last few months. We see that the premier of British Columbia is trying to extend the boundaries of his province into the Yukon and Northwest Territories. We see that the minister of revenue in the province of Quebec has said there are several departments in which there is too much overlapping and that as far as the federal field is concerned they could be done away with. We see the premier of Saskatchewan, after attending the meeting of the federal and provincial representatives,

certainly taking exception to the ideas which were voiced at that meeting. The premier of Saskatchewan was so incensed, evidently, by what took place that he felt that any change in the constitution, if Quebec was affected, would require the province of Saskatchewan to join up with the United States.
This of course is a most unusual approach. Those of us who know something of the economy of Saskatchewan and of the great potential there realize that in the years ahead the economic power of Saskatchewan will probably equal that of the province of Quebec. There are those tremendous deposits of potash which underlie so much of the area of Saskatchewan. The great potential in the province of Saskatchewan is not equalled anywhere else in Canada. Those minerals in the province which will be transported in ever increasing quantity to the underdeveloped and undernourished countries of the world will create an economy for Saskatchewan which will not be equalled. That is why I am wondering why the premier of a province such as Saskatchewan feels so concerned that after a federal-provincial conference he says that if certain other situations are prevalent Saskatchewan will also have to take some steps to dissociate itself from confederation. I am wondering just what did transpire in so far as the change in the constitution was concerned.
There are many people in all parts of Canada who have that same view, and I think it is only pertinent that we should at this time make some inquiry into and expect some explanations as to what the analysis of this whole situation can be. I am particularly concerned because I have heard in other quarters of people in public life who are concerned, and really concerned, about the attitude that was prevalent at that meeting.
One of those individuals is a constitutional lawyer of some note; in fact he is the former lieutenant governor of the province of Saskatchewan, Hon. Frank Bastedo. For the benefit of the committee I should like to put on Hansard tonight some of his opinions in this regard, because Hon. Frank Bastedo is recognized in most quarters as an eminent lawyer and one quite well fitted to analyse the situation as it prevails today. Mr. Bastedo was one of those who was a witness when the commission on biculturalism and bilingualism held its meetings in the city of Regina in the province of Saskatchewan. Mr. Bastedo was very concerned and some of his remarks illustrate his concern to some extent. He told those who were present that
